text: The assembly will now hear an address by
his excellency Rob Yetan, Prime Minister
and Minister for General Affairs of the
Kingdom of the Netherlands.
I request protocol to escort his
excellency and invite him to Andreas the
Assembly.
Mr. Presidents, your excellencies,
ladies and gentlemen,
and Frank was a teenage girl without
power or influence, but she had a pen
and a diary. A diary that would would
make its way into the world and inspire
millions of people. And I think that one
of the reasons people are so inspired by
an is that she had an unshakable belief
in the power of people to turn the tide
so that good prevails.
She wrote and I quote, "How wonderful it
is that nobody needs to wait a single
moment before starting to improve the
world." And these words are just as
powerful and true today. This week is
the perfect example of that. And I
realize that the United Nations does not
carry the most positive associations for
everyone. And indeed, there is much that
can and must be improved.
But let us not forget what lay behind
the founding of the United Nations over
80 years ago. The realization that doing
nothing had led to the darkest chapters
in human history. And we now live in a
different time. New generations have
arisen. and we face new challenges. But
when we look at the world today, we see
similar challenges as which preceded the
founding of the United Nations.
We see that the international legal
order is under pressure in more and more
places even though it is a very
foundation to our freedom and
prosperity.
We see the unending human suffering in
Gaza, Sudan, and so many other places in
the world. We see violations of
international law and of human rights
which are in stark contrast to the UN's
aims. And we see institutions being
undermined, institutions that were
established to protect people and
populations.
And we must not be naive about the
causes. These constant threats and
attempts to dismantle the legal order
are fueled by people and groups with
their own agenda. an agenda that runs
counter to the interest of everyone
else. Yes, everyone.
And even those who don't feel directly
threatened because they think it doesn't
affect them. Sooner or later, everyone
is affected as we saw in the time before
the United Nations. And when major
powers chose to pursue only their own
interest, it is tempting to respond
defensively. But as Mahatma Gandhi
thought, an eye for an eye will only
make the whole world blind. And so it is
time for us, the global community, to
choose to pursue the common interest,
not by trying to build an entirely new
world order, but simply by working
together. and the middle powers must
take the lead in fostering such
international cooperation and everyone
must be able to participate including
those countries who are currently too
often left on the sidelines. It is time
that countries in Africa, Asia and Latin
America at a fullyfledged place not only
on the equal earth map but in the real
world too. to start with here in the UN
improved African representation in the
security council at the very least
because
if we want
if we want to preserve the UN for the
future we must change the balance of
power in line with the changing times
and modernize our institutions and it
this means that we must focus on core
tasks and stable finance financing, but
also that we must work to protect the
multilateral order with all our
strength. And because international law
either works for everyone or for no one,
take the attempts we've seen to
undermine the international criminal
court, which is based in my country, in
my city. This undermines the
international legal order as a whole,
and that affects us all. This court was
established to protect us against
impunity. This court was built on the
foundations of the Nuremberg and Tokyo
trials. In the words of the Nuremberg
chief prosecutor Robert H. Jackson, and
I quote, "One of the greatest tributes
that power has ever paid to reason." And
now with the ICC under attack, the
writing is truly on the wall. After all,
how can you possibly be opposed to
prosecuting the very worst crimes? And I
believe there can be only one response
to say hands off the ICC and all those
other institutions that protect the
international legal order.
Because the reality
the reality is that we still need to
fight impunity not least through the
special tribunal for the crime of
aggression against Ukraine which the
Netherlands has offered to host in the
H. And let me be absolutely clear. We
cannot accept impunity in this fight.
Ukraine has no choice but to defend
itself. But Russia makes a choice every
day to wage war. And Russia must be held
to account for its flagrant violations
of the UN charter, for the immeasurable
suffering inflicted on so many victims
and families in this senseless war. And
since the downing of flight MH17, the
Netherlands has come to understand this
only too well. And many other others
understand it too, with Russia
threatening global food security and
millions of people experiencing the
consequences.
And history teaches us that the only way
to resolve conflict is through justice.
That was the idea underpinning the
establishment 80 years ago of the
International Court of Justice, the
principal judicial organ of the United
Nations. And it's a conviction that is
widely shared as illustrated by the fact
that more and more countries are finding
their way to the ICJ. So let us all
continue to stand up for what we have
built and strengthen it further as we go
forward. Ladies and gentlemen,
cooperation is the cornerstone of our
history and cooperation is what the
world expects of us now and in the
future. Take the question of how we
handle AI. We face a choice. Do we let a
small group of companies and countries
take all the decisions while the rest of
us simply look on? or do we decide
together within the logical setting of
the United Nations what our future
should look like? And it is also time
for us to press forward together and
tackle that other great challenge of our
time, climate change. Nowhere on earth
is a planet warming faster than in
Western Europe. But in the Caribbean
part of our kingdom, including the
countries of Aruba, Kurasau, and St.
Martin, the effects of climate change
have already been felt for much longer
and the same is true for many of your
countries. For too long, the
consequences of climate change have been
trivialized or simply denied. But after
the horrors experienced by Nepal and a
long series of forced fires, the truth
should be clear to everyone. The climate
crisis will not just disappear if we
pretend it doesn't exist. We are living
on bored time and the generations that
come after us will pay the price. And if
you want to prevail that, prevent that,
we must commit now to both mitigation
and adaptation. And we all know what
needs to be done. Countless reports are
agreed on that and we have all the
technology we need. And fortunately, we
are making progress. Last year, the
electrical vehicle markets grew by 20%.
Wind power capacity grew by 14% and
solar power by more than 30%.
And this growth in renewable energy has
exceeded even the most optimistic
projections from 10 years ago. And the
challenge now is to accelerate this
transition in all sectors and all parts
of the world. and at the same time to
reduce carbon emissions and phase out
fossil fuels. That is why the
Netherlands jointly with Colombia
organized the world's first conference
on transitioning away from fossil fuels.
This event in Colombia was attended by
57 countries and together these
countries account for onethird of global
GDP, onethird of energy demand and 1/5if
of supply. And together we worked to
find concrete and practical solutions to
take the transition forward. But climate
action requires everyone to contribute.
In November, we will gather at the COP
in Turkey. And I know that many of you
don't have high expectations. But in my
view, this can only be explained by the
pessimistic idea that we are somehow
powerless. But that is not true. We have
the knowledge and we have the technology
to combat climate change and a better
world is really within reach. Thanks to
our joint efforts on the sustainable
development goals, 92% of the world's
population now has access to
electricity. And since 2015, we have
doubled the amount of renewable energy
we generate. Child mortality has dropped
sharply too because of this access. So
climate action can be a catalyst for
everyone to work together on solutions
that concern us all. And we don't need
to reinvent the wheel. A lot of good
things are happening already. For
decades, the Netherlands has been
working with partners around the world
to develop climate smart agriculture and
futureproof water management solutions.
and we are keen to share our knowledge
and knowow and we want to learn from
what other countries are doing. There
are so many great initiatives on the way
but I also know there's much more to be
done. The need to accelerate and scale
up our efforts is only too clear and
that demands our common commitment. The
Netherlands wants to build practical
partnerships with other countries. So we
are once again making funding available
for this purpose and at the same time we
need to adapt to climate shocks that can
no longer be avoided. These adaptations
will require major investments both
public and private because here too we
cannot do it alone. Today I call on all
countries to stick to these ambitions
because one way or another a climate
transition is coming. But we can decide
how it unfold. It can be chaotic or it
can be carefully planned with an
inclusive approach and economic benefits
for all.
Ladies and gentlemen, as I come to the
end of my remarks, I have an even
stronger sense of what Anne Frank was
telling us because what she wrote is
true. We have everything we need to
change the world for the better. And we
don't have to wait another minute. We
aren't starting from scratch. We have
already come a long way. And the journey
will continue under the leadership of a
new secretary general.
Secretary General Gutierrez, thank you
for all your years of hard work. You're
leaving the United Nations at a
turbulent moment, but we can all take
pride in the fact that as we speak, more
than 150,000 men and women are serving
under the blue flag, giving
vaccinations, providing food aid, and
serving in peace missions. Even in this
difficult times when darkness seems to
be descending in many places on the high
ideals of the United Nations.
But the light has not gone out. The
torch of peace and justice still
flickers and guides us just as it did in
my country more than 80 years ago.
Liberation from tyranny of unbridled
nationalism, racism and fascism came too
late for Anne Frank and many others in
my country. When it did finally come, it
was brought by American, Canadian,
British, Polish and other allied
soldiers, many of them not much older
than Anne Frank. And among their many
resting places far from their homes, is
an American cemetery in Marata, a small
village in the south of the Netherlands.
A wall stands swatch over their graves,
and it is inscribed a simple epithes
we throw the torch be yours to hold it
high. Let us pledge as a new generation
to always hold it high. Thank you very
much.
On behalf of the assembly, I wish to
thank the Prime Minister and Minister
for General Affairs of the Kingdom of
the Netherlands.
